narrative:
The 2026 Colorado Rockies were a team that wore their struggles openly from the very first pitch of the season. Opening Day set an ominous tone when Victor Vodnik surrendered a home run that swung nearly 85% of win probability against the Rockies, and the early weeks became a parade of pitching disasters — grand slams, go-ahead doubles, and multi-run blasts that buried Colorado before they could ever find their footing. By the time May arrived, the Rockies had already established themselves as one of the most vulnerable pitching staffs in the National League, with a rotation and bullpen that routinely turned close games into lopsided defeats.

A remarkable turnaround emerged in late May and exploded through June, as the offense caught fire in a way that gave Rockies fans genuine reason to believe. Hunter Goodman became the heart of the attack, launching home run after home run, while youngsters Cole Carrigg and TJ Rumfield announced themselves as potential cornerstones of the franchise's future. A stunning stretch from late May through the Fourth of July holiday saw the Rockies rattle off some of the most impactful positive plays of the entire season — walk-off moments, clutch triples from Jake McCarthy, and Carrigg delivering back-to-back go-ahead shots that electrified Coors Field. For roughly six weeks, this felt like a team capable of something special.

But the summer heat brought a cruel reality check. The pitching — already the team's achilles heel all season — continued to bleed runs at an alarming rate, and the offense that had carried them through June couldn't sustain its torrid pace into August and September. Jaden Hill's implosion in late August and Jordan Romano's late-season meltdown bookended a painful collapse that confirmed what the numbers had been saying all along: this was a 58-104 ballclub, not a contender. The run differential of nearly 200 runs told the true story of a team that could score but simply could not stop anyone.

The 2026 Rockies will be remembered as a tale of squandered promise and youthful flashes. Hunter Goodman's power surge, Cole Carrigg's emergence, and a thrilling June run gave the fanbase something to hold onto, but the franchise's systemic pitching woes ultimately doomed any realistic playoff hopes. The season ends as a painful learning experience — one that will hopefully inform the front office's priorities heading into 2027, when the young core must be surrounded by the pitching infrastructure it so desperately lacks.

chapters.title: Disaster From the Jump
chapters.description: Colorado's pitching staff is torched repeatedly in the early going, as costly home runs and clutch hits against the Rockies set a bleak early-season tone.

chapters.title: Goodman Ignites a Spark
chapters.description: Hunter Goodman's back-to-back home runs on May 29th and June 1st signal the first signs of offensive life, giving the Rockies a reason to believe in their bats.

chapters.title: The June Surge
chapters.description: Carrigg, Rumfield, McCarthy, and Fulford join Goodman in a scorching stretch that becomes the defining highlight reel of the entire Rockies season.

chapters.title: Karros Carries the Flag
chapters.description: Kyle Karros caps the mid-summer high with a clutch three-run shot on July 5th, representing the last true moment of collective optimism before the wheels come off.

chapters.title: September Fade
chapters.description: A brief late-season bright spot from Brett Sullivan is sandwiched between two devastating pitching collapses, as Colorado's bullpen implodes and the season slips away for good.
